title: Your Body Actually Glows – You Just Can't See It ✨😮 #shorts
description:
In 2009, scientists from Kyoto University and the Tohoku Institute of Technology used ultra-sensitive cameras that detect single photons to film five young men in total darkness – and found that the human body gives off visible light about 1,000 times too faint for our eyes. The glow was dimmest around 10 a.m., brightest around 4 p.m., and strongest on the face, especially the cheeks. It is not body heat: the researchers think it comes from chemical reactions involving free radicals in our cells.

Sources: Kobayashi, Kikuchi & Okamura, PLoS ONE (2009), Live Science, National Geographic, NBC News

scenes.headline:
YOUR BODY
GLOWS IN
THE DARK

scenes.text: In 2009, scientists in Japan used cameras so sensitive they can catch a single particle of light.
They filmed five young men, sitting in total darkness for twenty minutes, every three hours.
And the men were glowing! But the light is about one thousand times too weak for our eyes.
scenes.label: TOO DIM TO SEE

scenes.text: The glow even follows a daily rhythm. Dimmest at ten in the morning, brightest at four in the afternoon.
The brightest part? Your face. Especially your cheeks.
And it's not body heat. Some of the warmest spots, like the neck, barely glowed at all.
Scientists think it comes from tiny chemical reactions in your cells. So yes, you are glowing. Just very, very quietly.
